headline: Buy at 18.5x forward PE and 4-4.5% yield; pay-per-lead pricing model structurally advantaged versus dealers
reasoning: Car Group's pricing model requires dealers to pay for leads whether or not a sale results, giving the platform structural pricing power. The company operates across five to seven countries with diversified revenue. At 18.5x forward PE and a 4-4.5% yield it represents better value than the other portal peers discussed. Francesco notes some overseas earnings mean franking is partial.
quote: This one's probably shown better value than the other two. I think, you know, trading on about 18 and a half times forward PE and yielding probably four to four and a half percent. Not fully frank, because obviously, you know, some of that overseas earnings has kicked in a lot. The thing I like most about car sales or car group, whatever they call themselves now, they operate in probably five, six, maybe seven countries. Is their pricing model. You know, I agree with everything Ben said, but their pricing model, speaking to a number of car dealers, they have to pay for leads. So even if someone looks at a car motor vehicle, let's say, for instance, you deal in second hand cars and you have someone go online and look at a particular vehicle. They have to pay for that whether they sell that car or not.

headline: Buy on defence spending supercycle; communications division (~65% of revenue) selling surveillance and comms to NATO-aligned defence forces, metal detection benefiting from gold price and mining demand, PE justified by earnings growth
reasoning: Codan is split roughly 60-70% communications and 30-40% metal detection. The communications division sells surveillance and non-offensive comms equipment to defence forces, emergency services, UN and Red Cross across 150 countries. NATO members committing to raise defence budgets from 1% to 2-3.5% of GDP are a multi-year demand driver. The metal detection division serves miners and airport security as well as retail consumers. Francesco discovered it via PEG ratio screening roughly two months ago and added it to model portfolios. The H1 profit guidance to more than double to at least $160m triggered analyst upgrades. At ~50x current earnings the PE is high but Francesco expects it to compress rapidly as earnings are upgraded. The company has been in operation since the 1950s and operates across 150 countries with a loyal institutional shareholder base including the founder's estate.
quote: This is a tech company. I came across it probably two or three months ago in my filtering and look, it was trading on about 40 times earnings. So expensive, but it's a tech stock... the communications division is probably about 60 to 70% of the business. The metal detections probably about 30 to 40% of the business. It is defence spending. So the theme in defence spending is big at the moment, particularly with, you know, Trump, you know, encouraging, if you like, some of the NATO countries to increase their defence spending. It's not bombs and bullets. So it's not offensive to some of these European countries. They can spend their money on communications and surveillance... They operate out of 150 countries. You know, they are selling to defence forces. They're selling to emergency services companies. They're selling to, you know, charitable organisations, UNs and Red Crosses and things like that for communication. So it's a big company. It's about, well, today, it's probably taking it over the $10 billion market cap size... we've got this in our model portfolio and I think there's still more upside in it because I still think there's more government spending on defence that needs to come.

headline: Hold; modest 4% earnings growth at 20x PE, 3% unfranked yield, leveraged to elevated interest rates via float income which is a fading tailwind
reasoning: Computershare trades on 20x for next year and 19.5x the year after, reflecting only modest earnings growth of around 4%. The 3% yield is unattractively low with zero franking. The business has benefited significantly from holding client cash at higher rates but that tailwind will fade. Corporate activity could be a positive catalyst, but currently M&A is taking companies off the ASX rather than adding them, which is a headwind to Computershare's registry business.
quote: We've got a hold recommendation. And going on what I've just been saying about some of these other marketplace companies, and computer share is not really a marketplace. It's a financial services register, if you like. It's trading on 20 times for next year and 19.5% for next. So there's not a lot of growth in their earnings. So I probably agree with the hold. The dividend is not that attractive at 3% zero franking. But look, things can change with the market. And if we start to see a lot of corporate activity, that can improve their earnings significantly.

headline: Buy ahead of REA; 20x PE, 4.5-5% fully franked yield, multi-country exposure means upside when employment markets recover
reasoning: Francesco prefers Seek to REA at current valuations given its 20x PE versus REA's 26x. Seek operates across approximately 11 countries, predominantly in Asia, providing diversification beyond the soft Australian job market. When employment markets turn around, earnings should re-rate from 20x to 30x. The 4.5-5% fully franked yield provides compensation for patience.
quote: Here's one, we just spoke about REA. It was about 26 times. This one's on 20 times. A very similar business. I would probably look at this ahead of REA at the moment because I think once you start to see the employment market turn around, these sort of businesses, you want to be looking at them when their market they're operating is under a bit of pressure because at some point, the employment market does turn around and then you're going to see significant growth. And instead of being trading on it 20 times, you're probably going to be looking at stop trading on 30 times. So, yeah, look, I like Seek... you're getting a yield of about 4.5% to 5% fully-franked. So, that makes it attractive if you're going to be patient as well.

headline: Hold at 16x and 4.5% fully franked yield; fairly priced versus QBE with less diversification and ANZ bank sale catalyst fully exhausted
reasoning: Suncorp trades at 16x versus QBE at 11.5x despite lower growth and less geographic diversification, making QBE the preferred insurer. The bank sale to ANZ has been completed and proceeds returned, so that catalyst is spent. The business is now a pure-play general insurer focused on a concentrated domestic market. If adding insurance to a portfolio, QBE is clearly preferred.
quote: We're exactly the same. We're a hold for the very same reasons. It's priced pretty fairly. And that's the difference between the two from an evaluation standpoint. Ultimately, as Ben mentioned, QBE has got more diversification. Suncorp, you can concentrate on more. The sale of the bank to ANZ, that's pretty much been fully realised and passed on to shareholders. So there's nothing more in that. So it's a much more focused business on the general insurance. But as Ben mentioned, it's a much smaller market that they're targeting. We're on 16 times at odds and a 4.5% fully frank dividend. I think it's just fair value. So if we're looking at putting insurance into your portfolios, I'd be going to QBE over Suncorp.

headline: Sell or lighten; 57x PE too high to call it oversold, no yield, and AI disruption risk real despite management adaptability
reasoning: At 57x earnings Xero is not cheap enough to justify a buy despite the recent weakness. Francesco disagrees with his own firm's analyst buy recommendation. AI will bring disruption to accounting software even if management can harness it for product improvement. With no yield there is no compensation for patience. He would wait for a lower entry level.
quote: I'm going to go against Ben here and against our analysts. Our analyst has a buy on it, and I don't agree. I think that 50 times to me is still too high to start looking at it from a point of view of being oversold. I agree with everything Ben said, it's a good platform and all that sort of stuff. But yes, there's going to be disruption with AI. I think people are misreading AI a little bit... But to me, at a 50, we got it on 56.8, so 57 times, no yield. If I was going to be patient with this one, I want some divvies. So I'd say wait, I think there's more downside in this one.

headline: Expects RBA to hike once more today then pause; property market slowdown and tightening consumer belts will stifle mortgage growth
reasoning: Francesco expects the RBA to raise rates at today's meeting but believes that will be it, largely because consumers tighten spending when property values decline even absent cash-flow impact. Tax regime changes are likely to prompt self-managed super funds to exit the property market, reducing mortgage growth prospects for banks. Consumer sentiment has plunged back to March lows, reinforcing the caution.
quote: I think at the rate rise, but that'd be it. Mainly because consumers really tighten their belts when it comes down to property. I mean, we've been through periods where we've had high inflation, unemployment's always been reasonably strong and higher interest rates. But I think with the tax changes and what we've seen happen with the property market, people tighten their belts when they see, yeah, my property is worth $1.5 million now, it's worth $1.4 million or $1.2 million, even though it's not a cash flow thing.

headline: Buy at 7.5x PE and 11.3% fully franked yield; streaming sport content via Stan and Nine Network is resilient, though Bruce Gordon's 30% stake removes takeover optionality
reasoning: Nine Entertainment is trading on 7.5x PE with a 11.3% fully franked dividend yield, which is reminiscent of GFC-era bank valuations. Streaming platforms are growing and sport content drives consistent viewership given its unpredictability. Stan and Nine's sport rights across rugby league, soccer and rugby are valuable assets. The main concern is Bruce Gordon's 30% holding via WIN, which suppresses takeover premium potential and raises governance questions about his strategic intent. Francesco would take a small portfolio weighting.
quote: The streaming platforms are doing well. You look at what these TV companies are paying for sport these days and you think, well, they're a bit heady. But then you get to understand that people were watching more sport than the traditional TV shows that they used to have, because there's so much unpredictability in sport... Then when I looked at the numbers, I mean, it's trading on a seven and a half times PE. Dividend yield of 11.3%, 100% fully framed. You look at those numbers and you go, well, I just mentioned CBA, you could have bought that towards the end of the GFC at those levels. Why wouldn't you buy nine entertainment?... I don't mind it. And I'll stick with the analysts. I think there's a buy there. Look, you're not going in with 100% of your portfolio, but I would consider it at the smaller end of the portfolio.

headline: Buy-rated but patient; would be more aggressive at 20x earnings; expects management change to improve pricing model along Car Group lines
reasoning: Francesco De Stradis has a buy recommendation on REA at Ord Minnett but is less enthusiastic than Ben Clark, flagging that acquisitions typically come at a premium and the share price reaction reflects that concern. He believes the stock looks attractive at 26x but would buy with much greater conviction at 20x. He sees the management change — bringing Car Group's pricing discipline — as a genuine medium-term positive. He does not view REA as a pure tech stock and notes it offers no meaningful yield. Overall he would be patient and wait for a little more weakness before increasing exposure.
quote: Probably not as optimistic. We do have a buy recommendation on at Ordmannet, so I'll probably stick with that, but I'll be I'll be a bit patient. I, I, I think there's probably a little bit more weakness. Ben's right, you know, trading on 26 times earnings, it looks relatively attractive. But at the same time, when you've got, you know, some fears of, of, you know, well, acquisitions to start with, generally you know, you pay more than you should for an acquisition, hence why the share prices off a bit today. But also, I think you're 26 times, you know, if you can get it at 20 times, you know, you'd probably buy it with your ears pinned back, 'cause I, I think, you know, the change in management structure will change the pricing, the way they price things.
episode_title: Stock of the day: REA Group (REA)

headline: Buy as market looks past near-term weakness to FY27 earnings recovery
reasoning: De Stradis noted the market is focused on the second-half recovery and looking ahead to FY27, with international sales having hit record levels the prior year and expected to pick up again. After the share price move ARB trades on about 21.5x earnings, falling to under 19x on next year's estimates, making it increasingly attractive. The Ord Minnett analyst team carries a buy rating, though De Stradis personally is not quite as bullish given lingering concerns around discretionary spending. Margins have been stabilising and the US business appears to be accelerating.
quote: I think the market's looking past it and going well. International sales in discretionary spending might pick up a bit. Um, it is trading on about 21.5 times uh, after this share price movement. Um, so it's still, you know, in what Luke saying, it's probably relatively inexpensive. Um, you know, there's some earnings growth into next year brings the PE back to under 19 times. So are starting to look more and more attractive. Um our analysts have a buy on it. Look, I wouldn't be as strong as that, but I do. I don't mind it. I'm just a bit concerned, um, around the discretionary spending side of things.
episode_title: Stock of the day: ARB Corporation (ARB)

headline: Francesco De Stradis sees Amotiv as offering better yield in the medium term due to its higher non-discretionary automotive parts exposure
reasoning: De Stradis flagged Amotiv as a motor vehicle parts and accessories stock that has had a rough 12 months but appeals because of its meaningful non-discretionary revenue — including brake pads, filters and maintenance essentials — which provides more resilience than ARB's more discretionary aftermarket accessories. While Ord Minnett does not formally cover Amotiv, De Stradis believes it will likely deliver a better yield in the medium term relative to ARB.
quote: A stock we don't cover at odds, but I don't mind in in the vehicle. Motor vehicle parts and accessory spaces are motive. Um, it's had a pretty rough trot over the last 12 months as well. Um, but what I do like about it, it has a fair bit of, uh, non-discretionary, um, um, automotive parts in it, you know, brake pads and filters and things like that, which are necessities for maintenance. So, um, whilst yes, we do like our arb, um, and, you know, we have a buy on it, I don't disagree with that. I wouldn't go as hard as that. Um, I think, um, a motive probably going to give you a better yield, uh, in the medium term, though.
episode_title: Stock of the day: ARB Corporation (ARB)

headline: Audenet likes EOS as a defence growth story with valuation upside after record order book guidance upgrade
reasoning: De Stratus from Audenet describes EOS as having transitioned from a turnaround story into a defence growth story, with the company consistently flagging record order books. The latest guidance upgrade reinforces that order book strength. Audenet's analyst valuation is $11.45 per share, which de Stratus acknowledges may be optimistic but believes there is definite upside from current share price levels.
quote: Yeah, look, we like this at Audenet. Look, EOS has transitioned from a turnaround story, I suppose, into a defence growth story. They've always, well, not always, recently stressed that they've got record order books. I think that upgrade sort of reinforces that order book that they have. Our analysts have got a valuation of $11.45 on it, which might be a bit optimistic, but where the share price is at the moment, I think there's definite upside in it.

headline: Analyst suggests the 'defensive no-brainer' narrative for quick service restaurants is now behind us as cost pressures evolve
reasoning: Commentary from Francesco de Stratus of Audemars suggests the era of QSR stocks being considered automatic defensive investments is over. Despite Collins Foods posting good numbers, the forward-looking view for the sector is more cautious, with analysts questioning the sustainability of QSR outperformance.
quote: The times when junk food, I'm sorry, quick service restaurants. Q-A-S-R. When they were like a no brainer defensive, I think that's behind us now.

headline: Aristocrat Leisure preferred over TabCorp; held in growth portfolio for quality and global diversification
reasoning: Francesco describes Aristocrat Leisure as a preferred alternative to TabCorp and holds it in his growth portfolio. It is not a great income stock but is a quality operator. It is internationally diversified unlike TabCorp and not as exposed to Australian regulatory risk.
quote: I'm a fruity aristocrat. We hold in a growth portfolio. You're not going to get a great deal of income out of it. It's good stock. Good operator. Light and Wonder would come in second on that, as in game developers. And they're not only exposed to the Australian regulatory environment, they're also global. So, you know, it gives them more opportunities, I think.

headline: CSL now looks cheap at current levels after de-rating from $300; underlying business quality unchanged
reasoning: Francesco uses CSL as an example of a quality business that became expensive at $300 but now looks cheap after selling off. He notes the underlying products and business quality haven't changed significantly despite some earnings growth concerns and a CEO change. He argues investors should distinguish between business quality and share price level.
quote: I think CSL is a high quality business. But look, at three hundred dollars, it was expensive. Now I think it's cheap. So but the underlying business hasn't changed much. Not really. Yes, they've had a few issues with some earnings growth or lack thereof and changed their CEO, which I think had to happen. But the underlying products and the quality of the business hasn't changed a great deal.

headline: Ebos Group a patient accumulate at under 14x earnings for Francesco as healthcare sector broadly offers good value
reasoning: Francesco agrees Ebos is a quality business and healthcare distribution stock, now trading under 14 times earnings going forward, which he sees as very attractive compared to historical multiples. He notes the whole healthcare sector globally has come under pressure including CSL, Cochlear and ResMed, all trading at valuations that would have seemed impossible a few years ago. He supports the view of taking a small initial position and being patient before adding more, watching for a broader sector turn in the next couple of months. He also highlights the 5.4% fully franked yield as rewarding patience.
quote: I tend to agree with Roger. I think a small position to start with is not too bad. I mean, I think the share price has come back a hell of a lot and it's probably presenting really good value. We have a trading on less than 14 times earnings going forward. So for, I would call it a healthcare stock. It is a healthcare stock, but it's really a sales and distribution wholesaler in the healthcare space. So you'd expect it to trade on a higher multiple, although healthcare stocks globally have come under a lot of pressure. We've seen CSL come off, Cochlear, ResMed, you name them. The big names even globally have all come off and they're all trading at multiples that you'd fall over yourself three years ago to buy them. Nowadays they're into hard basket. I think the whole sector is showing really good value.

headline: Ord Minnett has an Accumulate on Evolution Mining with attractive PE and 4% fully franked dividend for gold bulls
reasoning: Francesco notes Ord Minnett has an Accumulate recommendation on Evolution Mining, which he describes as a soft buy for those wanting to add gradually. The stock trades at around 14.5x earnings, which he considers relatively cheap for a gold miner if you expect the gold price to rise. It pays a 4% fully franked dividend for FY26 though analysts expect earnings and dividends to decline somewhat. He personally prefers Newmont as it is a lower-cost producer, meaning margins expand more with rising gold prices, but Evolution is still appealing.
quote: We have an accumulated recommendation on it. So that's a I suppose a soft type of buy, if you like. You know, if you've got some, you know, keep adding to it. You know, the copper angle on it. I mean, personally, I like copper, but you know, copper is a byproduct of the gold rather than gold being a byproduct of the copper. So look, it trades on a fairly attractive PE. So, you know, at 14 and a half times, you know, it's a round market. And I would expect, you know, a gold company, if you're expecting the gold price to rise, this looks relatively cheap, I would suggest.

headline: Goodman Group the preferred data centre and industrial property play for Francesco over Centuria
reasoning: Francesco recommends Goodman Group over Centuria for data centre and property exposure, describing it as the biggest and best in the space. He acknowledges it can get overvalued, which is why he also mentions Charter Hall as an alternative that doesn't become as expensive.
quote: I'm a Drudy, I'm probably more of a hold if you've been in there for a while. If I'm going to go down this path of a, and I'd call them not a property trust, I'd call them more of a property manager. I'd be looking at things like Goodman Group, they're the biggest and best in this space.

headline: Light & Wonder preferred over TabCorp for global gaming exposure and development pipeline
reasoning: Both Francesco and Rudy prefer Light & Wonder over TabCorp. Francesco says Light & Wonder is globally diversified unlike pure-play Australian wagering stocks, giving it more opportunities. Rudy echoes this preference strongly.
quote: Light and Wonder would come in second on that, as in game developers. And they're not only exposed to the Australian regulatory environment, they're also global. So, you know, it gives them more opportunities, I think. And if you want to get exposed to the local gaming market, I think it never is probably a good one.

headline: Francesco holds Medibank Private in income portfolio with soft buy below $5; defensive supported by mandatory health insurance regulation
reasoning: Francesco has a soft buy on Medibank, noting the price is around the right level but he'd be more comfortable buying below $5. He highlights that tax legislation effectively forces people into private health insurance, providing a structural tailwind. Customer growth is continuing with younger members participating. Revenue grew strongly in the first half of FY26 and outlook has not changed. He holds it in the income portfolio where it has been a stable contributor.
quote: If it comes back under $5, I'm happy to be buying it. It is a defensive and it's got to remember that the tax legislation forces people to be, you know, privately health insured. So that's a good thing for Medibank and other private health insurers. They're experiencing customer growth at the moment, coming from the company and younger member participation, which is interesting. I think younger people now are realising that, you know, and some of them because of their earning capacity as well, that they've been forced into taking out private health insurance.

headline: Ord Minnett's Francesco prefers Newmont over Evolution for gold exposure given superior margin leverage
reasoning: Francesco explains that larger, lower-cost gold producers like Newmont offer greater margin expansion as gold prices rise, because the fixed cost base amplifies the upside. He describes Newmont as the preferred pick for more conservative, larger-cap gold exposure versus Australian names like Evolution Mining.
quote: I prefer Newmont. OK, got it. NEM... your bigger miners like Newmont because they're the lower cost producers. The margins are a lot lower. So sorry, the margins are a lot greater. So as the gold price goes higher, they're not getting as much leverage as the smaller ones.

headline: Global healthcare sector broadly showing good value after significant de-rating including CSL, Cochlear and ResMed
reasoning: Francesco notes that major healthcare names globally including CSL, Cochlear and ResMed have all sold off significantly and are now trading at valuations that would have seemed impossibly cheap a few years ago. He views this as a broad sector opportunity, though he advises patience as he doesn't think the whole sector will turn around quickly.
quote: The whole sector is showing really good value. So I'd be a little bit patient on this. This is a smaller company than the likes of Sigma and Rudy mentioned the West farmers as well that's in this space. So I'd be patient at the moment now and let's see where it tracks over the next sort of couple of months before I'd add more to it.

headline: Pepper Money a sell for Francesco who sees 9.2% yield as a dividend trap with no visible capital growth
reasoning: Francesco views the 9.2% dividend yield as a trap because the share price chart shows continued deterioration with no floor in sight. He notes Pepper Money predominantly lends to property investors rather than owner-occupiers, making it more exposed to the tax environment changes affecting property investment. Without an Ords recommendation, he personally would not buy it and would sell if already holding, possibly using it as a tax-loss offset at this time of year.
quote: Any of the dividend yield, it's yielding 9.2%, but I think that's a dividend trap. I mean, if you look at that chart there, I'm no chartist, but I don't see any stopping on that. So I can see this at a much lower price. So if I owned it, I'd use it as a tax loss. I wouldn't be buying into it. I'd maybe watch it, see if these major shareholders might come back to the table, but I doubt it.

headline: Centuria Capital hold but Francesco notes AI data centre ambitions are risky and prefers Goodman Group for data centre exposure
reasoning: Francesco acknowledges Centuria's novel approach of providing the full data centre solution (what they call an AI factory) rather than just the shell, but says this adds more risk including on the critical issue of power availability. He doesn't agree with Ords' buy recommendation on it and would personally call it a hold for existing investors. He prefers Goodman Group as the biggest and best in this space, and also mentions Charter Hall as a good alternative that doesn't get as overvalued as Goodman.
quote: I think all property managers want to be data centres. These guys are a little bit different in that they, and they use the term AI factory. I think it's a bit, I won't say the word, but most data centres are a shell and then the data company will come in and put in their racks and their servers and all that sort of stuff. These guys are intending to provide the whole solution, which I suppose is novel. That to me takes on more risk as well. The biggest issue with these data centres is power. You can't put them in certain areas because they can't guarantee enough power to cool the data centres.

headline: Ord Minnett's Francesco rates Waypoint REIT a buy citing 7% yield, 32% gearing, near-100% occupancy and Viva Energy lease extensions
reasoning: Francesco describes Waypoint as one of Ords' preferred REITs. It yields 7%, trades at about 14x, has gearing of 32% which he considers within the normal 30-40% range, weighted average lease expiry of 6.4 years and near-100% occupancy. Most service stations are leased to Viva Energy, which has exercised a 10-year option on 21 sites. The company has also completed a $50m buyback. He is actively moving some client portfolios into property and Waypoint would be one name added.
quote: Waypoint is a good one. It's one of our preferred, if you like. It's yielding 7%. It's trading on a multiple of about 14 times. It's gearing levels of 32%, which I'm happy with. You know, 30 to 40 would be normal for a property trust. Any higher than that, I'd get a bit worried. The weighted average lease expiries are around 6.4 years and they're at almost 100% occupancy. So for me, it stacks up as a good property trust. Most of the service stations are Viva Energy. They've exercised a 10-year lease option on 21 of the sites. They're buying back some of the stock. I think they just completed about $50 million buyback. We have a buy recommendation. I probably agree with that.

headline: Francesco sees markets in a sideways pattern as Iran conflict and upcoming August reporting season create uncertainty
reasoning: Francesco believes the initial market pullback from the Iran conflict is likely the extent of the downside, as he thinks Iran lacks the firepower to sustain conflict and Trump wants a quick resolution before midterm elections. He expects markets to trade in a sideways range with wider-than-usual swings as geopolitical events drive volatility. He sees August reporting season in Australia as a key test, with confession season approaching. He notes the US reporting season showed positive signs but is uncertain whether Australian companies will follow suit.
quote: I think we saw the initial when the initial buying started, that pullback in the market, I think, was probably as far as we're going to go. I can't see it lasting too much longer. I think the Iranians will realize that they don't have the firepower to last them out. And I think Trump wants this to finish pretty quickly because midterm elections are coming up and he doesn't want that sort of going on in the background. So look, I think our markets are final level. I'll go up and down. The margins they move by are probably a little bit greater as bombs get dropped and peace treaties get signed. So I think we're destined for a bit of a sideways move at the moment.

headline: Ord Minnett's Francesco sees broad healthcare sector as undervalued with CSL, Cochlear and ResMed all trading at historically attractive multiples
reasoning: Francesco notes that globally healthcare stocks have come under significant pressure with CSL, Cochlear and ResMed all trading at multiples that investors would have eagerly paid much more for three years ago. He sees the whole sector as showing good value, even though it has become a 'hard basket' in terms of investor sentiment. He uses CSL specifically as an example, noting that at $300 it was expensive but now it is cheap, while the underlying business quality has not changed materially.
quote: We've seen CSL come off, Cochlear, ResMed, you name them. The big names even globally have all come off and they're all trading at multiples that you'd fall over yourself three years ago to buy them. Nowadays they're into hard basket. I think the whole sector is showing really good value.

headline: Ord Minnett's Francesco rates GrainCorp a buy at current levels with a $7.25 price target but warns it needs active management not buy-and-hold
reasoning: Francesco argues GrainCorp is trading well below fair value at current levels with an Ords price target of around $7.25. He says when the stock is cheap, as it is now, it is worth buying, but investors need to take profits on the way up rather than holding long term. Confirmed earnings for FY26 and a fully franked dividend provide near-term support. The company has also recently sold Grains Connect (Canadian assets) to consolidate. He acknowledges external factors like weather, El Nino, and global grain market politics are beyond management's control and create unpredictability.
quote: I think it's a buy at the moment. I think it's trading well below its fair value. Our analysts have got about $7.25 on it. I think that's pretty fair. If I bought it, I wouldn't wait till I got to $7.25 though before I exited... The thing that I think is the unknown elements of the external factors that can affect it, like you've mentioned, you know, the political events, the weather events and those sort of things, which, yeah, they have no control over. So, hence, when it's cheap, I think it's worth buying. And then as it rises, then I think you need to take profits.

headline: Middle East conflict and Iran tensions seen as the primary driver of market volatility heading into FY27
reasoning: Francesco sees the Iran conflict as the biggest global factor affecting markets, but believes the initial sell-off was likely the extent of the downside. He thinks Iran lacks the firepower to sustain a prolonged conflict and that Trump is motivated to resolve it before midterm elections. He expects markets to move sideways with larger-than-normal swings as geopolitical events unfold.
quote: Obviously, the biggest factor that's affecting our markets globally is the conflict in Iran. And as it heats up and peters out, the markets adjust. But I think we saw the initial when the initial buying started, that pullback in the market, I think, was probably as far as we're going to go. I can't see it lasting too much longer. I think the Iranians will realize that they don't have the firepower to last them out. And I think Trump wants this to finish pretty quickly because midterm elections are coming up and he doesn't want that sort of going on in the background.

headline: Audmanette's Francesco D'Astratus sees Goodman positioning as AI infrastructure and automated logistics play with high embedded expectations
reasoning: D'Astratus highlights that Goodman is positioning itself as the infrastructure player of AI, covering both data centers and logistics centers that are becoming increasingly automated with robotics. The absence of new contract announcements and high embedded expectations coming into the result led to slight market disappointment, though the business is tracking along satisfactorily.
quote: Problem with this company is there's a lot of embedded expectations. And with the absence of any announcements of new contracts and the high expectations leading into it, I think the market was slightly disappointed, but much of a muchness really, the businesses is tracking along okay. It's obviously caught up in the property bucket, but also, you know, now it's very much capturing the AI infrastructure, AI services theme as well. Goodman Gribb's positioning itself to be, I suppose the infrastructure player of AI, obviously data centers, but also logistics centers that they develop.
